content: CD2, also known as cluster of differentiation 2, is a cell adhesion molecule that is expressed on the surface of T cells and natural killer (NK) cells. It is also referred to by other names, including T-cell surface antigen T11/Leu-5, LFA-2, LFA-3 receptor, erythrocyte receptor, and rosette receptor. CD2 plays a role in cell adhesion by interacting with other adhesion molecules. In humans, it binds to lymphocyte function-associated antigen-3 (LFA-3/CD58), while in rodents, it interacts with CD48. These molecules are expressed on the surfaces of other cells. Beyond its adhesive functions, CD2 also serves as a co-stimulatory molecule, enhancing the activation and function of T cells and NK cells. CD2 is a highly specific marker for T cells and NK cells. This specificity makes it a valuable tool in immunohistochemistry for identifying these cell types in tissue samples. Additionally, the majority of T cell lymphomas and leukemias express CD2, which allows for the use of this antigen as a diagnostic marker to differentiate these malignancies from B cell neoplasms. Structurally, CD2 belongs to the immunoglobulin superfamily. Its extracellular region contains two immunoglobulin-like domains, which are characteristic of this protein family. CD2 has been shown to interact with several intracellular proteins, including CD2BP2, Lck, and PSTPIP1. These interactions are likely important for its signaling and functional roles in immune cell activity.
